* * * [T]he broadest delegation yet sustained and the one closest 
to the case before us came in Yakus, for the ultimate standard in the 
1942 statute was only that the maximum prices be “generally fair and 
equitable.”
Under these governing concepts we cannot say that in the Act 
before us there is such an absence of standards that it would be 
impossible to ascertain whether the will of Congress has been obeyed.
The court concluded that Congress’s will was well defined—and the 
President’s authority limited—by the text and legislative history of the Act, as 
well as by the historical context of previous administrative and judicial practice 
under wage and price control legislation enacted in 1942 and 1950. The 
legislation was enacted with careful attention to the broader pohtical and 
economic context, including the likelihood that action would be required when 
Congress was not in session. Viewed in that context, “this delegation was not 
an abdication by Congress, but the product of a reasoned analysis” that the 
delegation was necessary to “further the legislative purpose of stabilization.” 
Furthermore, the court noted:
It is also material, though not dispositive, to note the Hmited time 
frame established by Congress for the stabilization authority 
delegated to the President. The Act as enacted on August 15, 1970 
expired February 28, 1971, estabhshing a lifespan of about six 
months. Two subsequent extensions provided even shorter durations. 
When the ciu’rent expiration date of April 30, 1972, was set on May 
18,1971, Congress rejected the administration request for a two-year 
extension. Thus, in the words of the Government’s memorandum. 
Congress established a “close control.” It conjoined flexibihty in the 
President to act promptly with an obligation in Congress to 
undertake an affirmative review without prolonged delay, without 
the option of acquiescence by inaction.
The Union’s challenge to the legislation—and the court’s response to that 
challenge—also reveal that the non-delegation doctrine both protects the 
separation of powers and also limits government arbitrariness. Key to this dual 
function are the requirement of reasoned administrative decisionmaking and 
the availability of judicial review:
